metaDescription: Six Clarity amplified phones compared by boost from 26dB to 53dB, corded or cordless design, T-coil and Bluetooth, tone control and talking caller ID.
introParagraphs: Clarity is a brand that does one thing, and the line-up shows it. Almost every phone it sells is built around amplified sound, tone control and large, readable keys. That focus means a Clarity listing usually states a decibel figure and describes tone options, unlike general-purpose phones that mention volume boost in passing. It also means the range runs from a basic corded photo phone to a Bluetooth cordless that pairs with a mobile.

The six Clarity phones in this guide span amplification from 26dB on the corded P-300 to 53dB incoming on the corded AltoPlus. Between them sit a 30dB cordless with a T-coil, a 40dB DECT cordless with a digital answering system, an extra-loud cordless with talking caller ID and a 50dB Bluetooth model. Two more Clarity listings, the D704 and the E814CC, appeared in the same search, and we mention them where they help the comparison.

We evaluated the listings and buyer feedback and did not test the phones. Clarity phones are sold as comfort tools for people who find ordinary phones hard to hear, and an audiologist is the right person to ask about hearing needs or about compatibility with hearing aids.

products.name: Clarity AltoPlus Amplified Corded Phone
products.description:
The AltoPlus is the strongest amplifier in this group, and it is corded. The listing states that it amplifies incoming sounds by up to 53dB and outgoing speech by up to 15dB, which is unusual because most amplified phones boost only what you hear. A digital Clarity Power system is described as incorporating hearing aid technology for clearer call quality, and the ringer reaches 100 dBA.

The outgoing boost matters if the other person struggles to hear you, which happens with quiet voices or poor lines. Combined with the incoming figure, it makes calls easier on both ends. As a corded phone, it takes its power from the line on a standard connection, but check the manual for any feature that needs an adapter.

Compared with the Clarity P-300, it offers twice the incoming boost and a louder ringer but no photo keys listed. Compared with the XLC8, it is corded and does not pair with a mobile. If voice strength is the problem, this is the answer. Set the incoming boost to the lowest comfortable level at first, then raise it only as needed, since a clear voice at a moderate setting beats a loud, harsh one.
products.bestFor: People who need the strongest incoming boost and some outgoing help.

products.name: Clarity XLC8 Amplified Cordless Bluetooth Phone
products.description:
The XLC8 is the Clarity for people who want one phone to handle both a landline and a mobile. The listing gives up to 50dB of amplification with adjustable volume and four tone settings, and it can be used over a traditional landline or VoIP line as well as paired to a cell phone by Bluetooth. That means calls to a mobile arrive on the same large handset with the same boost.

Talking caller ID and a talking keypad announce the caller and the numbers pressed, which supports people with low vision as well. Check with the maker whether the boost applies to paired mobile calls as well as landline calls. Pairing needs a mobile phone, so confirm that yours supports it.

Compared with the AltoPlus, the XLC8 gives up a little boost for cordless freedom and Bluetooth. Compared with the D714, it has more boost and mobile pairing but no answering system listed. It suits households where the mobile is the main number. Pair the mobile in the same room as the base during setup, and keep the two within a short range afterward so the connection stays reliable.
products.bestFor: People who want mobile and landline calls on one boosted handset.
pros: Up to 50dB with four tone settings
Bluetooth pairing to a cell phone
cons: Requires a Bluetooth mobile for pairing

products.name: Clarity D714 DECT 6.0 Amplified Cordless Phone
products.description:
The D714, listed as the 53714, is the sensible middle of the Clarity range. The listing says it clearly amplifies incoming sound by up to 40dB, offers adjustable tone control and uses DECT 6.0 interference-free technology. It includes a digital answering system and, according to the title, works with VoIP phone service.

A 40dB boost with tone control is enough for most people who find ordinary phones too quiet, and the answering system means a missed call is not lost. DECT 6.0 avoids the busy Wi-Fi bands, which helps with clarity. The listing does not say how many minutes of messages the machine holds.

Compared with the XLC8, it has less boost but includes an answering system. Compared with the D712, it has more boost but the D712 adds a T-coil. A second listing for this phone describes it as a corded and cordless style set with one handset, so check which version you are buying. Read the listing carefully to confirm whether you are getting the cordless version or the corded and cordless style set before you order.
products.bestFor: A balanced Clarity with 40dB, tone control and a machine.

products.name: Clarity D712 DECT 6.0 Cordless with T-Coil
products.description:
The D712 is the Clarity to look at if you use a hearing aid with a telecoil. The listing describes T-Coil technology for clear calls, up to 30dB of amplification, an answering machine on the main handset and DECT 6.0. It starts with one main handset and can add up to four more, which are not included.

A T-coil lets a compatible hearing aid pick up the handset's magnetic signal directly. That can reduce background noise, but it only works if your aid has a telecoil and is set to use it, and the compatibility rating should be checked on the box. At 30dB, the amplification is lower than the other cordless Clarity phones, so someone who needs strong boost may prefer the D714 or the XLC8.

Compared with the D714, it trades ten decibels for the T-coil. Compared with the AltoPlus, it is cordless and expandable. It is for a hearing aid user with a telecoil who still wants an answering machine. Keep a spare handset charged in another room, because adding handsets later is easier than moving the base.
products.bestFor: Telecoil hearing aid users who want a cordless set with a machine.
pros: Expandable by up to four handsets

products.name: Clarity XLC3.4+ DECT 6.0 Extra-Loud Cordless
products.description:
The XLC3.4+ is the Clarity built around its ringer and its voice. The listing calls it an amplified cordless phone with an extra-loud ringer, big buttons and talking caller ID, using DECT 6.0 technology at 1.9GHz that is described as interference-free with wide range. A related bundle listing mentions talking caller ID in English or French and 30 percent more battery life.

The talking caller ID is the feature a household notices most. When a call comes in, the handset speaks the caller's name or number, so a person does not need to find the phone to know who is ringing. The extra-loud ringer is the other half of that plan. The listing does not give a decibel boost figure.

Compared with the XLC8, this one lacks a stated boost and Bluetooth. Compared with the D714, it has the louder ringer and a spoken caller. It suits someone for whom knowing who is calling matters as much as hearing them. If you buy a bundle with extra handsets, check that every handset in the box matches the base.
products.bestFor: People who want to hear who is calling before they pick up.

products.name: Clarity P-300 Amplified Corded Photo Phone
products.description:
The P-300 is the gentlest Clarity here and the easiest to set up. It amplifies incoming sound by up to 26dB, offers nine programmable photo memory buttons and gives control over ringer pitch and volume. It is corded, which means no battery and no base, and it keeps its list of features short.

The pitch control on the ringer is a small but valuable detail. Some people hear a lower tone better than a higher one, and being able to change it can make a difference. The photo buttons convert numbers into faces. The listing does not mention an answering machine, a speakerphone or a display.

Compared with the AltoPlus, it has half the boost and no loud ringer figure but adds photo keys. Compared with the XLC8, it has no mobile pairing. It is the entry point for a person with a mild need. Place it where the ringer can be heard from the main living area, and test the pitch setting with a family member on the first day.
products.bestFor: People with mild needs who want photo dialing and a tunable ringer.

buyingCriteria.criterion: How the Clarity range stacks by boost
buyingCriteria.explanation: The P-300 offers up to 26dB, the D712 up to 30dB, the D714 up to 40dB, the XLC8 up to 50dB and the AltoPlus up to 53dB incoming plus 15dB outgoing. The XLC3.4+ does not state a figure. Pick the lowest level that comfortably meets your needs, because high boost is not always clearer and very loud settings can distort. If you are unsure, an audiologist can suggest a target range. The numbers are not a ladder you must climb, so a person with mild needs gains nothing from the biggest figure.

The P-300 and AltoPlus are corded, while the D712, D714, XLC3.4+ and XLC8 are cordless with a powered base. Corded phones take their power from the line and keep working during a power cut on a standard line. Cordless Clarity phones give mobility but stop without mains power. Many households keep a corded Clarity beside the bed and a cordless one in the main room. Think about where the phone will live for the next five years, since most people settle into a favorite chair and a favorite room.

The D712 lists T-Coil technology, and the AltoPlus says its digital system incorporates hearing aid technology. A telecoil lets a compatible aid receive the handset's signal directly, but only if the aid has a telecoil and the setting is enabled. Check the compatibility rating on the box and ask your audiologist, rather than relying on a listing alone. Hearing aid makers publish their own immunity ratings, and adding the aid's rating to the phone's rating is the usual way to judge a good match. If you do not use a telecoil, a plain amplified phone may serve you better than paying for a feature you will never switch on.

Most amplified phones boost only incoming sound. The AltoPlus is listed with outgoing speech boosted by up to 15dB, which helps when the other person struggles to hear you. This matters for people with quiet voices or those who speak to relatives with hearing difficulty. If you are the one whose voice is hard to hear, this feature may matter more than the headline incoming number.

The XLC8 pairs by Bluetooth to a mobile and the listing hints that its amplification extends to mobile calls, which is worth confirming. Pairing lets you answer mobile calls on the large handset, which helps when the mobile is the family's main number. Confirm that your mobile is compatible and keep it near the base. Phones without pairing only work for landline calls.

The AltoPlus lists a 100 dBA ringer, the P-300 allows pitch and volume changes, and the XLC3.4+ and XLC8 offer talking caller ID. These details decide how easily a call is noticed and identified. Choose the aid that fits the specific difficulty, whether it is hearing the ring or knowing who is calling. A talking caller ID can be a relief for someone who cannot read a small display. Try the voice in a quiet room and in a noisy one, since some people find a synthetic voice harder to follow than a ring.

howWeEvaluated.title: Clarity match
howWeEvaluated.description: Only Clarity-branded phones were considered. The D704 and E814CC appeared in the same search and are mentioned for context, but we chose six with enough listing detail to compare.

howWeEvaluated.title: Boost range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated amplification from 26dB on the P-300 to 53dB on the AltoPlus, with the D712 at 30dB, the D714 at 40dB and the XLC8 at 50dB. The XLC3.4+ gives no figure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Design and power
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated corded and cordless models, since power behavior differs. The AltoPlus and P-300 are corded, and the four others need a powered base.

howWeEvaluated.title: Accessibility features
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted T-coil, outgoing boost, Bluetooth pairing and talking caller ID. The D712 leads on T-coil, the AltoPlus on outgoing boost, the XLC8 on Bluetooth and the XLC3.4+ on talking caller ID.

howWeEvaluated.title: Listing clarity
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed how much each listing told us. The AltoPlus and XLC8 are specific, while the XLC3.4+ and D714 have gaps or multiple versions, which we flag.

faq.q: Which Clarity phone has the most amplification?
faq.a: The AltoPlus lists up to 53dB on incoming sound and up to 15dB on outgoing speech. The XLC8 follows at up to 50dB. Both can be adjusted, so you do not need to use the maximum.

faq.q: Do Clarity phones work with hearing aids?
faq.a: The D712 lists T-Coil technology and the AltoPlus mentions hearing aid technology. Compatibility depends on your specific aid, so check the rating on the box and ask your audiologist. Try the phone with your aid during the return window.

faq.q: Can a Clarity phone answer my mobile calls?
faq.a: The XLC8 pairs by Bluetooth to a mobile phone and the listing suggests the amplification can apply to mobile calls, which you should confirm. Other models listed here handle landline calls. Confirm that your mobile supports Bluetooth pairing.
It makes your voice louder to the person you are speaking to. The AltoPlus lists up to 15dB of this. It helps when the person you call has trouble hearing you.

faq.q: Do cordless Clarity phones work in a power outage?
faq.a: Usually not, since the base needs mains power. A corded model such as the AltoPlus or P-300 can keep working on a standard line. Keep one corded phone if outages are a worry.
Yes. The D704 is a 40dB DECT phone listed for low vision, and the E814CC is a corded and cordless combo with an answering machine. Their listings give fewer details, so we did not feature them.

faq.q: How do I set the amplification?
faq.a: Use the adjustable volume and tone controls during a call with a familiar voice. Start low and increase until speech is clear, not just loud. Write down the setting so you can return to it.

faq.q: Is Clarity a good choice for someone new to amplified phones?
faq.a: Yes, because the brand focuses on amplified sound and usually states a boost figure. Start with a moderate model such as the D714 or the P-300, and move up if calls remain hard. Keep the return window in mind and test the phone with the voices you hear most.
